title: Strength Training Needs an Access Check
subtitle: A useful session begins with the person’s goal—not the gym’s default equipment, position or pace.
imageAlt: Two friends sit beside a strength-training station, discussing an adjustable setup before a workout.
imageConcept: an adult couple with one older family member together, in a specific visual scene about “Strength Training Needs an Access Check”: A candid, well-lit community gym scene: a wheelchair user and a friend sit at eye level beside an adjustable cable station, reviewing an equipment setup together; the friend listens rather than reaching in to adjust it.
body: Start with the person, not the program

Strength training is often presented as if everyone can use the same bench, grip a standard handle and follow the same sequence. For adults with disabilities, those assumptions can turn an otherwise useful workout into a series of barriers. The better starting point is a question: What would you like strength to help you do? The answer might be a sport, a transfer, pushing a wheelchair, carrying groceries, or simply feeling more capable in a chosen activity. It may also be a goal that has nothing to do with daily function. A recent American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) consensus statement emphasizes designing physical-activity programs around people’s individual circumstances, including disability-related considerations and barriers [1]. That is a framework, not a prescription for a single “adaptive” routine. Disabilities, bodies, preferences and training histories vary. The point is to build from the person’s aims and experience rather than asking them to fit an off-the-shelf plan.
Treat the guideline as a starting point

The CDC says adults with disabilities or chronic health conditions who are able should aim for muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups at least two days a week. It also advises consulting a health professional or physical-activity specialist about suitable activity types and amounts [2]. “If able” and “suitable” matter: a public-health target describes a broad direction, not a test someone must pass or a quota that overrides their circumstances. Start by asking what the person already does, what they would like to change, and what has made exercise difficult or uncomfortable before. Someone returning after a break, managing pain or fatigue, or learning unfamiliar equipment may need a different starting point from someone who trains regularly. The person’s own care team can help address medical questions; a qualified exercise professional can help translate a goal into a workable session. No one needs to disclose a diagnosis to justify asking for an accessible setup.
Make access part of the workout

Access is not a preliminary inconvenience to solve before the “real” training begins. It shapes what training is possible. Before choosing exercises, look at the whole route: Can the person enter and move through the space? Is there a clear place to position a wheelchair or other mobility aid? Can they reach and operate the equipment, adjust it, and get back out comfortably? Is there room for a support person if the trainee wants one? At a gym, it can help to ask staff about adjustable machines, alternate handles, accessible changing areas and whether equipment can be moved. At home, note the available floor space and which objects can be securely positioned. These are planning questions, not reasons to assume a person cannot use a particular setting. The person doing the training should lead decisions about what feels accessible and what changes they want to test. Ask before moving equipment, touching a mobility aid, or offering hands-on help.
Adapt the setup before abandoning the goal

Sometimes a change in position, grip, range of motion, resistance or equipment makes a movement more workable. ACSM describes anaerobic exercise as a way to build and maintain muscle and potentially improve some functional movements associated with disability [3]. Those examples are prompts for discussion, not instructions that every wheelchair user should train the same way. A useful sequence is to name the intended task, identify what feels difficult about the current setup, and test one adjustment at a time. Could the person use a different handle? Would a supported position or a resistance band fit better? Is there another exercise that works toward the same goal? Keep the person’s feedback central: an adaptation that looks convenient to a helper may be uncomfortable, tiring or simply unwanted. If a movement provokes unfamiliar symptoms or raises a medical concern, pause and seek appropriate professional guidance rather than trying to push through.
Plan a session that can change

A flexible session can be more useful than a fixed circuit. Before starting, agree on the exercises or tasks the person wants to try, what equipment is available and what would count as a comfortable stopping point. Decide how the person prefers to judge effort: for example, by how the movement feels, whether they can maintain their chosen technique, or another measure they already use with a qualified professional. Build in rest and the option to change the plan. Some people may prefer a short first session to learn the equipment and find workable positions; others may arrive with established routines. That cautions against treating a frequency guideline as a demand. If a session needs fewer exercises, a different order or more recovery, that is useful information—not a failure to train properly.
Make support an invitation, not an assignment

Friends and family can help make training easier, but support should be specific and agreed on. Ask, “Would it help if I called ahead about access?” or “Would you like me to stay nearby, or would you rather train on your own?” A person may want company, help carrying equipment, or a second set of eyes on a setup. They may want none of those things. A companion should not take over exercise selection, adjust a mobility device, lift or transfer someone, or provide physical assistance without permission and appropriate know-how. If hands-on help is requested, clarify exactly what is wanted and whether a trained professional should be involved. In a class or gym, the person training can choose what information to share and with whom. Respecting that control is not an extra courtesy; it is part of making exercise genuinely accessible.
Use a simple check-in to improve the next session

After trying a movement or a full session, take a minute to review it together—if the trainee wants company. Ask what felt useful, what got in the way and what they would change next time. Keep the notes concrete: “The handle was hard to reach from this position,” or “More rest between sets helped.” Record only details the person wants kept, and let them decide whether a friend, trainer or clinician sees them. Patterns can help distinguish a one-off equipment problem from a setup that consistently needs adjustment. They can also make a conversation with a qualified professional more focused. The ACSM consensus statement summarizes barriers to physical-activity participation and recommendations for programs tailored to adults with disabilities [1]. The useful lesson is to pay attention, adapt, and avoid claiming one session proves what will work for everyone.

Choose one goal the person themselves cares about and one setting they would consider using. Before the next workout, ask what would make that setting easier to enter, position in and use. Write down any equipment or access questions to ask the gym, trainer or relevant professional. Agree on what support—if any—a companion should provide, and leave room to change the plan once the person tries it. The first session can be about learning one piece of equipment or finding a comfortable starting position; it does not need to demonstrate a complete program. If a medical condition, new symptoms or uncertainty about safe movement complicates the plan, bring that question to an appropriately qualified health professional. Then let the person decide what to test next. Strength training becomes more workable when access, choice and adaptation belong to the program from the beginning.
